text.p: Texaco Inc. said Friday that potential plaintiffs in the $176.1 million settlement of a racial discrimination suit should not mistakenly believe the company wants them to opt out of the agreement.

The statement is contained in the proposed notice be sent to class members that was filed Friday along with the tentative settlement plan in White Plains federal court. The proposal still requires a judge's signature before it can be considered for final approval at a Feb. 27 fairness hearing.
Lawyers said slight changes in the proposal may be made next week before U.S. District Judge Charles Brieant is expected to sign the tentative accord.

The class consists of all African-Americans employed in a salaried position by Texaco or its subsidiaries at any time from March 23, 1991 through Nov. 15, 1996. They have a Feb. 20 deadline to opt out of the settlement.
The proposal includes the notice to be sent to the potential class members.
"Texaco believes all class members should feel absolutely free to benefit from the settlement and should not mistakenly believe that Texaco prefers that class members opt out," the notice says.

Texaco said in the notice that unless a class member plans to pursue a separate employment discrimination claim against the company arising prior to Nov. 16, it knows of no reason for an individual to opt-out.
Although Texaco denies fault, it agreed on Nov. 15 to pay $176.1 million to settle the 1994 lawsuit filed by black employees who alleged they were discriminated against in pay and promotions.

The case received wide-spread attention after transcripts of tape recordings submitted as evidence in the proceedings showed executives allegedly discussing the destruction of documents and making racist remarks.
On Wednesday, Texaco announced it had fired a top executive of an insurance subsidiary and had taken actions against other current and former employees who can be heard on the tapes.
The move came after the company received a final report from an outside lawyer who investigated the situation.

As part of the settlement, White Plains, N.Y.-based Texaco developed a plan to boost employment, career development and recruiting of minorities, as well as increasing purchasing from minority- and women-owned companies.
The plan was well-received by lawyers representing the black plaintiffs and the Rev. Jesse Jackson, who responded by calling for an end to a consumer boycott of Texaco he helped initiate in November.
Under the agreement, Texaco previously deposited $115 million in an escrow account, upon which interest is accruing.
When the settlement becomes final, each class member will receive an 11.34 percent increase over his or her Nov. 15, 1996 base annual salary retroactive to Jan. 1, 1997.
The settlement also provides for intervention by the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission following an agreement reached last week between Texaco and the EEOC.
Under the accord, the EEOC will have certain rights to receive information, monitor the lawsuit settlement, and participate in court proceedings.
Texaco's stock gained $2 to $106.875 in late trading on the New York Stock Exchange.
